claims.text: The tribo-corrosion response of high-entropy alloys is governed by competition between mechanical disruption of a passive oxide film and the film's repassivation ability.
Faster repassivation kinetics reduce overall degradation under combined wear and corrosive conditions.
The initial high-entropy alloy naturally forms a protective passive oxide film in a neutral environment.
Alloy composition can be modified to vary passive-film repassivation rates.
Testing under inert and corrosive environments while holding mechanical loading and sliding conditions constant can separate pure wear from coupled wear-corrosion behavior.
The relevant structural mediator is the integrity and kinetic recovery of the passive oxide film.
Mechanical wear removes sections of the passive film and exposes bare metal.
Rapid repassivation reforms a protective layer over exposed areas and minimizes degradation.
Slow repassivation leaves exposed areas susceptible to accelerated corrosion.
Alloys optimized for rapid repassivation will have lower total tribo-corrosion degradation than a matched alloy with slower film recovery.
Rapidly repassivating alloys will exhibit less corrosive damage than a matched alloy with slower film recovery.
Rapidly repassivating alloys will also exhibit reduced wear relative to a matched alloy with slower film recovery.
Under inert wear conditions, only mechanical wear contributes to material loss.
Repassivation governs the coupled response under moderate wear and corrosive conditions when additional degradation mechanisms are absent.
The proposed governing effect may fail when mechanical loading overwhelms repassivation kinetics.
The proposed governing effect may fail at high temperatures because temperature can alter passive-film properties.
Wear volume, electrochemical impedance, and corrosion current density can be used to test the proposed relationship between repassivation and degradation.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome defines the matched baseline as a different alloy with slower film recovery under corrosive conditions, whereas the baseline field defines it as the same alloy under inert, non-corrosive wear. These are distinct controls and make the stated relative predictions ambiguous.
